posts.text:
I think Michael Burry is wrong to sell $FNMA and $FMCC common.

And I think Bill Ackman has the better map of how this ends.

Burry's Oct 11 note is clear: he sold the common, bought junior preferred, and flagged a Treasury conversion of the senior preferred (SPS) into common — dilution of 90%+.

That risk is real on paper.
I just don't think it's the base case the Trump team is trying to deliver.

Here's why I side with Ackman:

1. The SPS has already been paid — economically.

Fannie and Freddie drew about $193B from Treasury after 2008.
They have since returned about $301B in dividends.

Ackman's point is simple: treat the senior preferred as repaid, don't invent a brand-new dilution event to wipe out private common holders.

2. Ackman's path preserves the common.

His three-step plan:
→ Treasury / FHFA amend the PSPA so the SPS is treated as satisfied
→ Treasury exercises its warrants for ~79.9% of the common
→ Relist on the NYSE while conservatorship continues

Government control stays.
Mortgage markets aren't disrupted.
Existing common isn't vaporized by a 90% conversion.

That is "walk before you run," not "convert and crush."

3. Burry is hedging a scenario Ackman is fighting.

Burry's move makes sense if you believe Wall Street's conversion base case wins.
Preferred ranks above common if that happens.

But if the political goal is to show taxpayers a win, rebuild tradable equity, and keep housing finance quiet — converting SPS into a 90% wipeout of private common is a terrible headline.

It's the path that creates lawsuits, not a clean listing story.

4. Price action isn't the thesis.

Both stocks have given back most of the post-election rally.
Burry reads a head-and-shoulders.
I read a messy policy delay in a narrow AI-dominated market.

Weak charts don't settle who owns the economics of the GSEs.

My takeaway

Burry is brilliant at smelling risk.
Here, I think he's underweighting incentives.

A conversion that destroys private common may look neat in a spreadsheet.
It looks ugly in an administration that wants to claim it fixed Fannie and Freddie.

Ackman's framework asks a better question:
How do you end conservatorship without blowing up the mortgage market — and without stealing the residual that private capital already paid for once?

On that question, I think Ackman is closer to right.

$FNMA $FMCC

Sources:
Burry, Cassandra Unchained (Oct 11, 2026)
Ackman / Pershing Square commentary on the three-step GSE plan and SPS repayment

We are witnessing a historic shift.

The annual spread between the S&P 500's earnings yield and the 10Y Note yield is down to -1.5 percentage points, its lowest since 2009.

Since 2022, this yield difference has fallen -440 basis points, its largest 5-year decline since the 1970s.

As a result, the S&P 500's equity risk premium is on track to post its 3rd consecutive negative annual reading, the longest streak since 2002.

This suggests that, on a yield basis, theoretically less risky 10Y Treasuries are now more attractive than the S&P 500.

In other words, investors are receiving a higher yield from Treasuries than from the S&P 500, despite the additional risk of owning stocks.

Historically, a negative equity risk premium has been associated with strong risk appetite and stretched equity valuations.

We expect an eventful Q4 ahead.

Model Benchmarks Are Worthless 

How can a model score 24% and 59% on the same 113 coding tasks?

It happens when you vary the harness that wraps it. 

I’ve increasingly ignored most of the recent model leaderboard results. Partly from exhaustion and partly because improvements in a ranking don’t show up in the actual work. 

So I asked the 8090 Labs team to measure what the leaderboards skip: the model and the harness together, on real bug fixes and features from open-source projects.

8090 Labs ran 7 models through 5 harnesses. 

Here are a few results I didn't expect:

- Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 scored 41% in Claude Code and 61% in OpenAI's Codex. It made 28 tool calls at the median in one and 66 in the other.

- The cheapest runs weren't the cheapest work. GLM in Codex cost $0.22 a run and $0.93 per success. In Pi it cost $0.25 a run and $0.43 per success.

- GLM passed a task on both attempts 51 times in one harness and 16 times in another.

- GPT-5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6 barely cared which harness they were in.

The bottom line is that if you're picking a model/harness combo off a model-only leaderboard, you're making a critical decision based on only half the information.

https://www.8090.ai/blog/same-model-different-harness?dub_id=5Ux9L6PBuBjhKzi7

I presume you are engaging in good faith. And therefore it seems you may have simply missed the word “unfunded” in my post. 

As your various replies have mixed large *unfunded* commitments that might be non-cancellable with smaller real *funded* commitments ($35b, $18b). 

The supply chain takes the *funded* commitments seriously.

Thank you for all the work you have done over the years.

quoted.text:
Ed, the $35 billion deal with Apollo and Broadcom is definitionally “funded.” The supply chain takes funded commitments like this one seriously.

It is the ~$1 trillion of unfunded commitments based on vague MOUs that almost no one in the actual supply chain treats as real.

That distinction is the whole point.

As far as I can tell, most of the people who take the ~$1 trillion in unfunded commitments seriously are AI skeptics, which is ironic.

Good luck - I have enjoyed reading some of your work over the last year.
